extracted.intended_audience: logicians, philosophers, scientific writers, and developers of scientific/technical terminology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing and maintaining a philosophical/scientific vocabulary: how to fix meanings, provide descriptive terms, avoid fallacies introduced by connotation, and use conventions and scales to enable precise observation and induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve historical meanings; require historical knowledge before altering
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Whoever seeks to introduce a more correct use of a term with which important associations are connected, should be required to possess an accurate acquaintance with the history of the particular word, and of the opinions which in different stages of its progress it served to express.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting to change a term's meaning, ascertain the word's history and the opinions previously expressed by it; avoid redefining in ways that make formerly accepted propositions false unless you have considered all previous usages and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let parts of a word's meaning drop inadvertently
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It may be good to alter the meaning of a word, but it is bad to let any part of the meaning drop.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing or modernizing usage, ensure that you do not accidentally abandon aspects of meaning that are still valuable or that underpin earlier true propositions; be careful not to lose useful semantic content through casual drift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms must convey a determinate and unmistakable meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That its terms shall each of them convey a determinate and unmistakable meaning.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A philosophical/scientific language's primary requisite is precision of meaning for each term—ambiguity undermines investigation. Prefer words with single, well‑fixed senses when used for scientific purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No important meaning without its word (lexical completeness for important concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There should be no important meaning without its word. Whatever we have occasion to think of often, and for scientific purposes, ought to have a name appropriated to it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that every concept frequently encountered in observation, experiment, or theory has a dedicated term so that records and communication can be exact and efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate Descriptive Terminology for recording observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive Terminology: names need to exist to make records of individual observations that exactly show what fact has been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a precise vocabulary that permits unambiguous recording of observed instances (e.g., botanical or mineralogical terms). This includes naming elementary sensations, recurring combinations, and distinctive features so that an observation's wording maps closely to what was perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate names of elementary sensations with direct perceptual exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The meaning of [descriptive] technical terms can be fixed in the first instance only by convention, and can be made intelligible only by presenting to the senses that which the terms are to signify... the term refers to the sensation, and not to the parts of the term.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For elementary sensory terms (colors, basic textures, etc.), teach meanings by giving direct sensory examples or standards (color swatches, specimens). Such names cannot be fully defined verbally; they must be learned through perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix technical terms by convention and exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical terms are fixed by convention and made intelligible by presenting the sensory instance they signify (e.g., 'apple-green', 'tin-white').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing technical vocabulary, tie the term to a convention and a concrete exemplar to avoid vagueness; the user should recall the intended sensation or property immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name frequent combinations for brevity and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Combinations of sensations or feelings may always be described, if we have a name for each of the elementary feelings... brevity of description, and clearness... are greatly promoted by giving distinctive names not to the elements alone, but also to all combinations which are of frequent recurrence.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If particular combinations of properties recur often (e.g., botanical forms, compound features), coin concise terms for them to improve descriptive efficiency and clarity rather than always composing long descriptions from primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions for composite/compound terms but recognize limits for elementary sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘When the thing named is... a combination of simple sensations, it is not necessary... that the student should refer back to the sensations themselves; it may be communicated to him through the medium of other words; the terms... may be defined. But the names of elementary sensations... can not be defined.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define higher‑order or compound technical terms in words; however, avoid attempting to define base sensory terms verbally—use perceptual teaching for these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and preserve standardized scales and numerical measures where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Werner's classified scale of colors; Mohs' numerical scale of hardness; specific gravity as a numerical measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For properties that admit ordinal or quantitative comparison (color classification, hardness, specific gravity), adopt standard scales and numerical systems to enable precise communication and comparison across observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and guard against semantic drift from ignorant misuse and translation errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Language degenerates by ignorant misuse (e.g., 'transpire' used for 'to happen', 'aggravating' for 'provoking', 'predicate' for 'predict'), and by careless translation (e.g., 'demander'→'demand').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and resist vulgarisms and mistranslations that widen or corrupt terms' senses; recognize when common misuse has become entrenched and either adapt definitions consciously or work to preserve the technical distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid question‑begging names and connotative bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Words expressing moral or social facts often carry connotations of approval or blame; such connotations give rise to the fallacy of 'question‑begging names' where mere use of the name assumes the disputed property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When naming phenomena in moral, political, or evaluative domains, avoid using terms whose ordinary connotation already assumes the point in dispute. If unavoidable, explicitly note the connotative bias and define the term neutrally for argumentative purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When changes in usage are irrevocable, define words according to new meanings and retain old meanings as secondary senses
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The logician... should submit to them with a good grace when they are irrevocably effected, and if a definition is necessary, define the word according to its new meaning; retaining the former as a second signification...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If usage has permanently shifted, adopt the contemporary meaning in definitions used for communication, but record and preserve the former meaning when useful (e.g., as historical or philosophical senses) to avoid loss of conceptual resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure descriptive terminology supports induction (need for general names)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘But when we proceed from this to Induction... we stand in need of an additional and different sort of general names.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond specific descriptive terms for individual observations, create general names (class/generic terms) that facilitate grouping and comparison of instances for inductive reasoning. The vocabulary must serve both description and abstraction.
